extracted.intended_audience: readers of political philosophy and constitutional criticism; legislators and educated public concerned with the effects of the French Revolution on government and representation
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical political essay arguing how constitutions and representative institutions should be constituted and constrained, using the French Revolution as a negative example; emphasizes property, virtue, and institutional checks. It assesses who should govern, how representatives should be chosen, and what social arrangements preserve liberty and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative character and previous stake in society
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme authority should not be placed in the hands of men 'not taught habitually to respect themselves' and 'who had no previous fortune in character at stake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men drawn suddenly from humble ranks will be intoxicated with unprepared greatness and pursue private interests at the expense of the state. Representatives should have established character and stakes (fortune, rank, or proven virtue) so they can bear responsibility and moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid domination by narrow professional habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblies dominated by a single profession (e.g., law or medicine) are ill-suited to govern a state because professional habits disable broader understanding of mankind and mixed affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawyers are described as 'meddling, daring, subtle, active, of litigious dispositions' who, if they preponderate, will make law for self-interest and create a 'litigious constitution.' Doctors and other professionals 'are rather disabled than qualified' for comprehensive statecraft. A legislature should be mixed and not overrepresented by any one faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of fundamental laws and constitutional constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislature must be restrained by fundamental law, strict conventions, and respected usages; absent these, a constituted assembly can remake the constitution to its own designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The National Assembly's lack of 'fundamental law, no strict convention, no respected usage to restrain it' makes its power absolute and dangerous. Good government requires institutional checks (counterpoise like a House of Lords and prerogatives of the crown) to prevent arbitrary remaking of the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must reflect ability as well as property (property predominant)
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate representation must represent the nation's ability and property, with property being predominant because it is the 'natural rampart' defending other interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability is vigorous and active; property is sluggish and must be predominant in representation 'out of all proportion' to resist invasions by ability. Representation that does not secure large property interests risks plunder and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect concentration of large property holdings
rubrics_metrics.description: Large aggregations of property should be put beyond the possibility of danger because property is by nature unequal and concentrated wealth forms a defensive rampart for society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diffusion of the same quantity of property among many weakens its defensive power; dispersal makes each person's portion a temptation and invites plunder. Institutions should secure the perpetuation of family property as a social good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of hereditary property and institutions to secure transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of perpetuating property in families (hereditary wealth/distinction) is one of the most valuable circumstances for society and tends to the perpetuation of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hereditary property holders are 'the natural securities' for transmission of property; the House of Peers, composed of hereditary property and distinction, serves as ballast for the commonwealth and ultimate judge of property divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit (virtue and wisdom) as sole qualification for office
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'no qualification for government but virtue and wisdom, actual or presumptive.' Wherever these are found, they should be admitted to place and honor regardless of birth or station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While admitting talent from any class, the essay insists merit must be proven: 'If rare merit be the rarest of all rare things, it ought to pass through some sort of probation.' The road to eminence should not be too easy; virtue is tried by difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject sortition/rotation as general electoral methods
rubrics_metrics.description: No rotation, no appointment by lot, no mode of election operating in the spirit of sortition or rotation can be generally good in a government dealing with extensive objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such methods fail to select a man suitable to the duty; they do not tend to accommodate the office to the person. Governments of large scope require selection targeted at aptitude, not random or purely rotational systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of levelling/equalizing social order
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to 'level' society do not equalize but 'change and pervert the natural order of things'; certain descriptions of citizens must be uppermost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associations of trades (tailors, carpenters) are not fit to occupy elevated political positions. Some regulated preeminence (preference, though not exclusive) for birth and rank is 'neither unnatural, nor unjust, nor impolitic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve public honors, ranks, and distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some decent, regulated preeminence and preference (not exclusive appropriation) given to birth and distinction is legitimate and useful for public affections and national pride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honors and rewards ('prizes of honor and virtue') keep the 'mind' of the country alive; destroying the organs of the state and distinctions extinguishes public dignity and emulation, harming social cohesion and recovery after turmoil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid government by those selected for private advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Men elevated by chance or self-interest (e.g., money-jobbers, usurers, stock-dealers) will pursue private rapacity and the destabilization of property if permitted to govern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns that dealers in stocks and funds will seek to exchange paper wealth for land and that men whose habits are in chicane will pursue lucrative jobs following convulsions, undoing stability; leaders should be chosen to prevent such predation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization in a single city threatens national unity
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution that creates many independent municipal republics with one dominant capital (e.g., 'the republic of Paris') will dismember the country and cannot be governed as one body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An eighty-three-municipality republican system risks provincial resistance to central monopolization of spoils and power; no single mind will impel the whole country—localism undermines national governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions and conventions define civil rights; rights of man are not absolute within civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: If civil society is the offspring of convention, then convention limits rights; rights claimed as absolute (the 'rights of men') cannot override the conventions making society possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One fundamental motive of civil society is 'that no man should be judge in his own cause.' Rights incompatible with civil society (e.g., unchecked self-governance) are repugnant to its existence and must be set aside by convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in adopting foreign revolutionary examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncritical admiration of foreign revolutionary models (France) can lead to palliating atrocities and importing dangerous principles unsuitable to another nation's constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay cautions against imitating French practices (e.g., radical equal representation, abolition of orders) on the assumption that their example is 'favourable' to 'exertions in the cause of liberty'; policies must fit national circumstances and long experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid economic policies that substitute unstable paper circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'paper circulation' and a 'stock-jobbing constitution' are symptoms of destroyed property and rational liberty; compulsory paper currency and reckless monetary experimentation are dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacing legal coin with compulsory paper currency and employing plundered public revenue in maintaining rival armies or feeding urban populations risks national bankruptcy and debauchery of military and civic institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders of reform should aim to elevate not to destroy
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who lead change should 'sanctify their ambition by advancing the dignity of the people' with long views, aiming to rule and improve rather than merely to destroy their country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts are drawn between destructive demagogues and leaders like Cromwell or Sully who, though nursed in turmoil, aimed to illuminate and beautify the world. Ambition must be balanced with public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware demagogic theorists who treat ancestral practice as worthless
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculatists who despise experience and treat long-standing constitutional forms as illegitimate ('the rights of men' admitting no prescription) threaten stability by rejecting precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay criticizes those who would blow up 'all examples of antiquity, all precedents, charters, and acts of Parliament' on theoretical grounds; prudent governance respects tested institutions and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must be judged by practical adequacy, not merely formal equality
rubrics_metrics.description: The common notion that representation must be numerically equal is dismissed; representation should be adequate to the purposes for which it is devised, not simply 'pure and equal' in theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author challenges democratist claims that inadequate representation renders government illegitimate; he contends the existing system has been 'perfectly adequate' for its practical ends and that accusations of illegitimacy are fallacious.
